hostSignals.claimText: Glyphosate has remained one of the world’s most widely used herbicides due to industry influence on the regulatory process.
Regulators largely assess glyphosate by itself, in isolation, rather than testing the commercial products people are actually exposed to.
Commercial formulations of glyphosate can be up to a thousand times more toxic than glyphosate alone due to additional ingredients.
Regulators do not require long-term toxicity testing of complete glyphosate formulations.
Even minuscule doses of glyphosate herbicides can result in serious disease over time, including cancer.
Regulatory agencies do not take into account the cocktails of pesticides that people are exposed to daily.
The current acceptable daily intake of glyphosate is clearly inaccurate or wrong, according to Antoniou.
Antoniou's laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
Regulators need to completely reassess their position on glyphosate safety due to the influence of industry data.
The same biological pathway targeted by glyphosate exists in many bacteria and fungi, including those in the human gut microbiome.
Independent studies often receive little or no attention compared to industry-sponsored research, which influences regulatory decisions.
Antoniou criticized the growing use of glyphosate as a pre-harvest drying agent, which leads to glyphosate residues in the food supply.

mintedClaims.claimText: Glyphosate has remained one of the world’s most widely used herbicides due to industry influence on the regulatory process.
Industry’s influence extends from the studies regulators rely on and the products they test to the exposure limits they consider safe.
One of the biggest flaws in glyphosate regulation is that agencies largely assess glyphosate by itself, in isolation, instead of testing the commercial products people are actually exposed to.
Regulators do not require long-term toxicity testing of complete glyphosate formulations.
Even minuscule doses of glyphosate herbicides can result in serious disease over time, including cancer.
Independent studies often receive little or no attention compared to industry-sponsored research, which influences regulatory decisions.
Regulatory agencies do not take into account the cocktails of pesticides that people are exposed to daily.
The current acceptable daily intake of glyphosate is clearly inaccurate or wrong, according to Antoniou.
Antoniou's laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
Regulators need to completely reassess their position on glyphosate safety due to the influence of industry data.
Antoniou criticized the growing use of glyphosate as a pre-harvest drying agent, which leads to glyphosate residues in the food supply.
The same biological pathway targeted by glyphosate exists in many bacteria and fungi, including those in the human gut microbiome.
The gut microbiome plays a vital role in digestion, immune function, cardiovascular health and nervous system signaling, Antoniou said.
Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as “absolutely safe,” Antoniou said.

If regulators evaluated the complete formulations instead of glyphosate alone, Antoniou said allowable exposure limits would have to be drastically reduced, and uses in homes, parks and other urban areas would likely be banned.

Regulatory agencies rely on laboratory animal toxicity studies to set their so-called safe exposure limits, but the criteria by which a given animal toxicity study is eligible to be considered were set by industry.
As a result, independent studies often receive little or no attention, even when they clearly have no conflicts of interest, Antoniou said.
That’s how influential industry has been, he said.
Even if regulators relied on stronger science, they would still be evaluating glyphosate under conditions that don’t match the real world, Antoniou said.
But you and I, we’re all exposed to cocktails of pesticides on a daily basis, he said.
This is another reason why our regulators are letting us down, Antoniou said. They’re not protecting us properly.
Manufacturers encourage farmers to spray wheat, barley, oats, rye and other crops just days before harvest so the grain dries more uniformly and can be harvested sooner.
The result is that glyphosate residues are going straight into the humans’ food supply, he said.
According to Antoniou, industry has long defended glyphosate by arguing that it targets a biological pathway found in plants but not in humans.
But that argument overlooks a critical piece of biology, he said.
Research from Antoniou’s laboratory and others shows glyphosate can disrupt those microbial communities, contributing to gut imbalance and the onset or the occurrence of leaky gut.
Monsanto clearly ignored this mechanism of toxicity, he said.
Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as absolutely safe, Antoniou said.
His laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
In one study, animals developed liver disease after long-term exposure to glyphosate concentrations 125,000 times below the European Union safety limit and 250,000 times below the U.S. safety limit.

packets.localResponseWindow: In an interview on “ The Corbett Report ,” Antoniou outlined what he sees as the biggest failures that have kept the “deceptively toxic” herbicide on the market despite a growing body of independent research linking it to serious health risks. packets.claimUnits: According to Antoniou, industry has long defended glyphosate by arguing that it targets a biological pathway found in plants but not in humans.
packets.localResponseWindow: But that argument overlooks a critical piece of biology, he said. The same pathway exists in many bacteria and fungi, including microorganisms that make up the human gut microbiome . Research from Antoniou’s laboratory and others shows glyphosate can disrupt those microbial communities, contributing to gut imbalance and “the onset or the occurrence of leaky gut.” The gut microbiome plays a vital role in digestion, immune function, cardiovascular health and nervous system signaling, Antoniou said. “Monsanto clearly ignored” this mechanism of toxicity, he said.
